name: Natural musk and scent on skin theory

lead: The theory holds that a person's natural scent, sometimes called body musk, is part of attractiveness, and that perfumes and deodorants can mask it, clash with it or enhance it. Followers aim to keep their own smell appealing and pick products that work with it.

Body odor is produced mainly when skin bacteria break down apocrine gland secretions, and it varies with genetics (such as ABCC11 and MHC genes), diet, health and medication. Some studies link odor to immune-gene differences in mate preference, though the evidence base for human chemical signaling is limited and debated.

paras: Followers choose lighter or fewer fragrances, keep up regular washing, and sometimes wear scents on skin so they blend with their natural smell. Diet and clothing hygiene are also discussed as influences.
No direct harms are tied to the belief. Reviews note that human pheromone claims remain disputed, and body odor can also reflect health, diet or medication.

angle.text: Proponents say your own body scent is part of how attractive you come across, and that fragrance can mask or enhance it. General research shows odor varies with genes, diet and skin bacteria, but the attraction claim itself has not been tested.

lead: The natural musk and scent-on-skin theory is the belief in appearance communities that a person's own body odor, and how a chosen scent interacts with their skin, is a meaningful part of attractiveness. Proponents frame natural scent as a signal that perfumes or deodorants can mask or enhance.

Human body odor is produced mainly when skin bacteria act on secretions from apocrine glands, and it is influenced by genetics, diet, health and medication.[1] Researchers have reported links between body odor and immune-gene (MHC) differences in mate preference, although the evidence base for human chemical signaling is limited and debated.[1][2]
infobox: Skin microbiome, apocrine glands, genetics (ABCC11), MHC genes[1]

paras: Humans have eccrine glands from birth and apocrine and sebaceous glands that become active at puberty. Apocrine glands, concentrated in the armpits, secrete the compounds that skin bacteria turn into odorous molecules.[1]

Corynebacterium species produce butyric acid-type compounds associated with rancid or cheese-like smells, and Staphylococcus species produce thioalcohols and isovaleric acid. Propionic acid from sebaceous ducts is found pleasant by some people at low concentrations.[1]

The ABCC11 gene largely determines underarm odor. A loss-of-function variant, common in East Asian populations and rare in European and African ones, is associated with less odor and lower levels of the steroids androstenone and androstenol.[1]

sections.h: Musk in perfumery versus body musk
paras: Musk originally meant a secretion of the male musk deer, whose main odorant is muscone. Nearly all musk in modern fragrance is synthetic, in aromatic nitro, polycyclic and macrocyclic classes.[3] Perfumery musk is a distinct topic from human odor, and Wikipedia's musk article does not link it to human glands.[3]
Within the scent-on-skin theory, the word musk is used loosely for a warm, skin-like scent, and some believers use the term for the perceived natural smell of a person.

Studies cited on Wikipedia report that women's sense of smell is strongest around ovulation and that women tend to prefer male odors from people with MHC/HLA types different from their own, which may favor offspring with stronger immunity.[1] Body odor also carries information on kinship, age and possibly sexual orientation, and the direction of cause is unclear for the last.[1]

Androstenone is the first mammalian pheromone identified, in boars, but there is little scientific support for it as a human pheromone, and its smell varies widely between people owing to receptor variation (OR7D4).[2] A research review states that no pheromonal substance has been shown to directly change human behavior, a position that is disputed.[4]

No studies found testing whether wearing or leaving off scent changes perceived attractiveness in real-world settings through the mechanism proposed by the theory. Laboratory work on MHC and odor preference and on pheromone candidates is summarized above.[1][4]

Deodorants reduce odor with alcohol, antibacterials and fragrance, while antiperspirants block sweat pores. Daily washing reduces skin bacteria, and one study cited on Wikipedia linked higher fruit and vegetable intake in men to more pleasant-smelling sweat.[1] About 90 percent of Americans reportedly use deodorants or antiperspirants.[1]
